intro/hello: Welcome to linear classifiers. This is the chapter where our classifiers stop memorizing, and start to learn.
intro/knn: Last chapter, the nearest neighbor classifier kept every single training image, and compared each new image against all of them.
intro/slow: That works, but it is slow at test time, and it never really learns anything. It just remembers.
intro/idea: This chapter introduces the idea that the rest of the course is built on.
intro/score: Instead of remembering the training set, we write down a score function, with a few adjustable numbers inside it. Those numbers are called the parameters.
intro/loss: Next to it, a loss function: a single number that measures how bad the scores are.
intro/learn: And learning becomes a search: find the parameter values that make the loss small.
intro/start: The simplest score function of all is one matrix multiply. That is where we start.
score/img: Take one image from see-far ten. It is thirty two by thirty two pixels, with a red, a green and a blue value in each.
score/count: That makes thirty two times thirty two times three values, which is three thousand and seventy two numbers.
score/flat: Stretch them all out into one long column, and call it x.
score/want: We want ten numbers back: one score per class, where a high score means, this image looks like my class.
score/W: A linear classifier gets them with one multiplication. W is a grid of weights: ten rows, one per class, and three thousand and seventy two columns, one per pixel value.
score/wname: Why weights? Each one sets how much its pixel value counts toward the class's score, like weighing evidence.
score/mult: W times x walks along each row, multiplies every weight by its matching pixel value, and adds up the products. Ten rows give ten numbers.
score/b: Then we add b: ten biases, one per class, added at the very end.
score/bname: Why bias? Show it an all-zero image and the score is just b: the class's built-in lean before any evidence.
score/thresh: The 1958 perceptron had a threshold the weighted sum had to beat. Move it to this side of the equation, and it becomes b.
score/out: Out comes a column of ten class scores. Right now W is random, so the scores are tiny noise.
score/params: The image is given. W and b are the parameters: the numbers we get to choose.
score/goal: Choose them well, and the correct class gets the highest score. Here is the same image after training: ship wins.
score/fast: And once they are learned, the training images can be thrown away. Classifying a new image costs just one multiply.
by-hand/toy: To watch the multiply up close, shrink the image to just four pixels: fifty six, two hundred and thirty one, twenty four, and two.
by-hand/three: And keep three classes: cat, dog and ship. So W has three rows of four weights, and b has three biases.
by-hand/cat: Start with the cat row. Zero point two times fifty six is eleven point two.
by-hand/cat2: Minus zero point five times two hundred and thirty one is minus a hundred and fifteen point five. Then plus two point four, and plus four.
by-hand/catb: That totals minus ninety seven point nine. Add the cat bias, one point one, and the cat score is minus ninety six point eight.
by-hand/rows: The other rows work the same way. Dog scores four hundred and thirty seven point nine, and ship scores sixty point seven five.
by-hand/dot: In NumPy, W dot x, plus b, does all twelve multiplications at once.
by-hand/wrong: Now suppose this image really is a cat. Then these weights are bad: dog wins by a mile, and cat comes last.
by-hand/vote: Read each weight as a vote. A large positive weight says: a bright value here is evidence for my class.
by-hand/neg: A negative weight says the opposite: a bright value here is evidence against me. The cat row puts minus a half on the brightest pixel, and that is what sinks it.
geometry/point: Here is a useful way to picture what W does. Every image is a single point, in a space with three thousand and seventy two directions, one per pixel value.
geometry/two: We cannot draw that many directions, but the idea survives perfectly in two. So here are points with just two numbers each, from three classes.
geometry/zero: Take the blue class. Its score is exactly zero along a straight line: positive on one side, and negative on the other.
geometry/arrow: Its row of W is an arrow, at a right angle to that line, pointing toward the side where the score grows.
geometry/turn: Turn the arrow, and the line turns with it.
geometry/bias: The bias does something different. It slides the line back and forth, without turning it.
geometry/all: Every class gets its own line, and its own arrow.
geometry/argmax: Each point goes to the class whose score is highest there.
geometry/regions: And that carves the plane into regions, with straight borders between them.
geometry/walls: That is all a linear classifier can ever do: cut space with flat walls. In three thousand and seventy two dimensions the walls are still flat, just harder to picture.
templates/second: There is a second, more visual way to read W.
templates/fold: Each row holds exactly one weight per pixel value. So it can be folded back into a thirty two by thirty two color picture.
templates/line: The score for a class then measures how well the image lines up with that picture: big where both are bright together.
templates/tpl: So each row is a template for its class. Classifying an image means checking it against ten templates, and picking the best match.
templates/learned: Here are ten templates, learned from just one thousand real see-far images. With so few, they stay blurry, but the gist is there.
templates/blue: Plane and ship turned blue: sky and water.
templates/green: Bird, deer and frog went green and brown, the colors of grass and forest. And car leans red.
templates/horse: One template per class is a real limit, though. A horse facing left and a horse facing right have to share a single picture.
templates/match: Hand it our ship, and the ship template gives the best match.
templates/acc: On new images, it gets about one in three right: far better than the one in ten you would get by guessing.
bias-trick/clumsy: Keeping track of W and b separately is a little clumsy. A common trick folds them into one array.
bias-trick/one: Add one extra number to the end of every image, always equal to one.
bias-trick/col: And glue b onto W, as one extra column.
bias-trick/why: Now the last weight in each row gets multiplied by that constant one, which is the same as simply adding it.
bias-trick/same: Same scores, but one parameter array instead of two, and every formula after this gets shorter.
bias-trick/raw: One more habit, before we grade the scores. Raw pixels run from zero to two hundred and fifty five.
bias-trick/center: So first, we center the data. Compute the average image over the training set, and subtract it from every image.
bias-trick/around: Now every pixel value is spread around zero: some positive, some negative.
bias-trick/scale: Often each value is also scaled into a range like minus one to one. Chapter eight explains why this matters so much for training.
grading/have: We have a way to produce scores. Now we need a way to say how good they are.
grading/three: Here are scores for one image. Cat, three point two. Dog, five point one. Ship, minus one point seven. And the image really is a cat.
grading/fn: A loss function takes the scores and the correct answer, and returns a single number.
grading/lossname: The word comes from decision theory: a loss is the price paid for a bad decision, so lower is better.
grading/hilo: High when the scores are bad, and low when they are good.
grading/train: Training will mean nudging W and b to make that number smaller.
grading/two: The course introduces two classic choices: the SVM and the Softmax. They agree on what a perfect answer looks like, but disagree, interestingly, about everything else.
svm/wants: First, the multiclass Support Vector Machine loss, or SVM. It wants the correct class to beat every other class by at least a safety margin, called delta. Usually, delta is one.
svm/line: Picture it on the bars. Draw a line one delta below the correct score.
svm/intrude: A wrong class that pokes above that line is too close for comfort, and the loss grows by how far it intrudes.
svm/dog: Dog scores five point one: past cat itself, and well past the line. Its gap is five point one, minus three point two, plus one, which is two point nine.
svm/ship: Ship scores minus one point seven, comfortably below the line. Its gap is negative, so it costs nothing at all.
svm/hinge: That is the job of the max with zero: keep the intrusion if it is positive, and zero otherwise. Flat, then rising. This shape is called a hinge.
svm/self: The correct class does not compete with itself, so its own margin is set to zero.
svm/sum: Add up what is left, and the loss for this image is two point nine.
svm/formula: In symbols: sum over every class j except the correct one, the max of zero and s j, minus s y, plus delta.
svm/raise: Now raise the cat score. As cat pulls ahead, the dog's intrusion shrinks, and so does the loss.
svm/happy: Once every wrong class is below the line, the loss is exactly zero. The SVM is completely satisfied, however close the race actually is.
regularization/subtle: There is a subtle problem with the SVM loss.
regularization/zero: Suppose some W gets every training image right, with every margin met. Its loss is exactly zero.
regularization/double: Now double W. Every score doubles, so every gap doubles, and the loss is still zero. Ten times W works too.
regularization/tie: The loss alone cannot tell these apart. So we break the tie with a preference for small, spread out weights.
regularization/l2: The most common choice is L two regularization: square every weight, add them all up, and multiply by a knob called lambda.
regularization/full: The full loss is the average data loss over all the training images, plus this regularization loss.
regularization/square: Squaring punishes big weights much more than small ones.
regularization/example: Take an input of four ones. The weights one, zero, zero, zero give a score of one. So do four weights of a quarter each.
regularization/pick: But their squares add up to one, versus a quarter. Regularization prefers the second, which spreads the effort and uses all of the evidence.
regularization/knob: In practice, that also works better on new images. Lambda is a hyperparameter: it trades small weights against fitting the data.
regularization/onlyW: And notice: it is only ever applied to W, never to b.
softmax/second: The second classic reads the scores as probabilities.
softmax/problem: Scores can be any number, positive or negative. Probabilities must be positive, and they must add up to one.
softmax/moves: The softmax function makes that conversion in two moves.
softmax/exp: First, exponentiate every score: raise e, about two point seven one eight, to the power of that score.
softmax/pos: That makes everything positive. Ship's minus one point seven becomes zero point one eight.
softmax/bigger: And it makes big scores much bigger, since each extra point of score multiplies by about two point seven. Cat becomes twenty four point five, and dog, a hundred and sixty four.
softmax/divide: Second, divide each one by the total, so they add up to one.
softmax/pie: Now every class gets a slice of a pie. Cat, thirteen percent. Dog, eighty seven. Ship, almost nothing.
softmax/formula: In symbols: p k is e to the s k, divided by the sum of e to the s j, over every class j.
softmax/sharp: The slices of higher scores are disproportionately larger. A lead of one point nine in score became a lead of almost seven to one in probability.
softmax/softname: The name is literal: a soft maximum. The top score gets most of the probability, but every class keeps some, so it changes smoothly instead of jumping.
cross-entropy/look: The softmax loss looks at one thing only: how much probability landed on the correct answer.
cross-entropy/neglog: It takes the log of that probability, and flips the sign. This is called the cross entropy loss.
cross-entropy/ours: Our cat got zero point one three, so its loss is about two point oh four.
cross-entropy/certain: Here is the whole curve. Certain and right, with probability one: the loss is zero.
cross-entropy/half: A fifty fifty hedge costs about zero point six nine.
cross-entropy/tiny: Only one percent on the right class costs four point six, and the loss grows without limit as that probability heads to zero.
cross-entropy/never: Unlike the SVM, it is never fully satisfied. There is always a little more probability to squeeze onto the correct class.
cross-entropy/explode: One practical warning. Exponentials explode. e to the thousand is too large for a computer to store, so the division turns into nonsense.
cross-entropy/shift: The fix is free: subtract the largest score from all of them first.
cross-entropy/cancel: Every exponential gets multiplied by the same constant, which cancels in the division. The probabilities do not change, but now the largest exponent is e to the zero, which is one.
compare/same: So how do the two compare? Give them the same scores, and push the cat score up.
compare/start: At three point two, cat is losing, and both losses are clearly unhappy.
compare/svm: As cat pulls ahead, the SVM loss falls in straight lines. Once the margin is met, it hits zero and stays there. It stops caring.
compare/soft: The softmax loss keeps shrinking too, but it never quite reaches zero. It always wants a little more.
compare/read: They also read the scores differently. To the SVM, scores are raw numbers, and only the margin matters.
compare/prob: To the softmax, scores are unnormalized log probabilities. So it hands you probabilities, with a grain of salt: how sharp they are depends on lambda.
compare/practice: In practice, the two perform about the same. Softmax is more common today, because probabilities are handy.
recipe/shape: The deeper point of this chapter is the shape of the recipe, which every remaining chapter reuses.
recipe/one: One: a score function with parameters. Here, W x plus b. Later, a deep network.
recipe/two: Two: a loss function that grades the scores. The SVM or the softmax, plus regularization.
recipe/three: Three: an optimization procedure, which adjusts the parameters to lower the loss. That is the next chapter.
recipe/recap: And remember the two readings of W. Each row is a flat wall between classes, and a template picture of its class.
recipe/next: Next comes optimization: how to find the W that makes the loss small, by walking downhill on it, one small step at a time.
